Explain the idea behind the Fourier transform and what the amplitude and phase of the DFT represent.
risposta: The Fourier transform expresses a signal as a weighted sum/integral of sinusoids of different frequencies; Fourier series handle periodic signals while the Fourier transform extends this to non-periodic ones over a continuous spectrum. The transform F(omega)=R+iI is complex, encoding amplitude A=sqrt(R^2+I^2) and phase phi=atan(I/R) per frequency. For images, the DFT amplitude tells how much of each frequency is present but lacks spatial information, while the phase encodes the spatial arrangement (location of edges, lines, corners, textures). Reconstructing from phase alone still gives a recognizable but distorted image, showing phase carries most structural information.

domanda: Describe how a 2D Fourier spectrum of an image is interpreted (center, frequencies, orientation).
risposta: The 2D spectrum F(u,v) is usually displayed with the zero frequency (DC, the average intensity) at the center. Low frequencies near the center correspond to large-scale, smooth structures; high frequencies far from the center correspond to fine details, edges, and texture. The orientation of lines in the spectrum corresponds to edge orientation in the image, but rotated 90 degrees: e.g. vertical edges produce horizontal lines in the frequency domain.

domanda: State the convolution theorem and explain how it enables efficient filtering, including low/high/band-pass examples.
risposta: The convolution theorem states that convolution in the spatial domain equals element-wise multiplication in the frequency domain: F{g*h}=F{g}.F{h}. So instead of an expensive spatial convolution you can FFT the image and kernel, multiply them element-wise, and inverse-FFT the result. This makes frequency-domain filtering intuitive: a low-pass mask preserving central (low) frequencies blurs (a Gaussian is an excellent low-pass filter); a high-pass mask attenuating low frequencies sharpens or detects edges; a band-pass ring mask isolates features of a specific scale.

domanda: Compare box and Gaussian filters in the frequency domain, and explain hybrid images.
risposta: A box filter is abrupt in space; its Fourier transform is a sinc with strong sidelobes, giving an imperfect cutoff and ringing artifacts. A Gaussian is smooth in space and its transform is also a smooth Gaussian, giving clean attenuation - which is why Gaussian is preferred for blurring. Hybrid images combine the low-frequency content of one image (via a low-pass/Gaussian filter) with the high-frequency content of another (via a high-pass/Laplacian filter) and add them; the result is perceived as the low-frequency image from far away and the high-frequency image up close.
